Write implementation plans for five units of the Nexus Code v1.3.0 release: PF-3, PF-4, SB-1, MT-2, PA-2. Write one file and nothing else: `/home/mike/nexus-wt/_plans/PF_SB_MT_PA_PLAN.md` (one top-level section per unit). Do not edit code. Work read-only against `git -C ~/nexus-code show origin/release/v1.3.0:<path>` / `git -C ~/nexus-code grep <pattern> origin/release/v1.3.0 -- <paths>` (fetch first). Do not ask the user questions: where something is undecided take the plan's stated default, or else the conservative option, and record it under "Decisions taken".

Sources: `docs/v1.3.0/PLAN.md` on that branch (read it all: the unit rows; gates G-1..G-7; decisions D13 (npm publish: default "no publish; the entry point is documented but not published"), D22 (profile names and defaults: default "ship `:workspace`, `:read-only`, `:network`; interactive default stays today's engine defaults until an explicit profile is set; managed policy may force a stricter profile, never a looser one") and any other decision these units cite; the phase ordering; the peer-project notes at the top, including the Codex re-read on permission profiles and the tool registry). Existing plans for style and depth: `/home/mike/nexus-wt/_plans/AC1_PLAN.md`, `VR2_PLAN.md`, `GV1_PLAN.md`.

The units, verbatim acceptance from the plan (re-read them there):
- PF-3: transport beyond a parent's stdio: a unix domain socket (default) with a token and origin check for any localhost HTTP/WebSocket listener; several clients may attach and reattach. Acceptance: a second client attaches to a running session; a wrong token is refused; the socket is mode 0600.
- PF-4: library entry point: a `lib` entry that does not run commander on import, `exports` and `types` in `cli/package.json`, a package name decision, a documented minimal embedding example that spawns the sidecar. Acceptance: an example script runs a verified task through the entry point in CI.
- SB-1: named permission profiles that map today's bwrap/docker flags, HOME mounts and network settings without loosening gates; profiles compose with approval mode and managed policy; `nexus doctor` and session posture print the effective profile; document residual holes honestly. Acceptance: CLI and doctor show the effective profile; a profile cannot disable verification-path protection, grant allow-always, or bypass G-3; existing sandbox tests stay green.
- MT-2: tools are registered spec+handler pairs (a registry: spec and handler bound together); dispatch and G-3 suites green. It follows MT-1 (the `agent.ts` split, landed in v1.2.1): confirm what MT-1's acceptance was and whether anything of MT-1 is left, and say so.
- PA-2: conflicting units fail verification on the merged tree ("verified merge arbitration" for parallel operation units): read the PA-1/PA-3/PA-4 docs under `docs/v1.3.0/` and `cli/src/core/operation*.ts`, `cli/src/batch.ts`, `cli/src/loop.ts`, worktree handling, to define what a "unit", a "merge" and "verification on the merged tree" are here.

Existing building blocks to reuse (verify each by reading; cite file:line): the sidecar server and protocol (`cli/src/sidecar.ts`, `cli/src/protocol.ts`, `docs/protocol/`), `ApplicationCore` (`cli/src/core/app.ts`), the ACP adapter's bounded line reader and request correlator (`cli/src/acp/jsonrpc.ts`), `cli/src/index.ts` (commander program; how it is structured and what importing it does today), `cli/package.json`, `scripts/package-linux.sh` and the package smoke tests, the sandbox (`cli/src/sandbox.ts`, bwrap and docker engines, `cli/test/verify_sandbox.test.ts`, `sandbox_*.test.ts`), `nexus doctor` (`cli/src/doctor.ts`), managed policy (`cli/src/core/managed_policy.ts`, `policy_runtime.ts`, `docs/MANAGED_POLICY.md`: `sandbox.*` keys), the capability registry and definitions (`cli/src/core/capability_definitions/`, `capabilityRegistry`, `cli/src/core/dispatch_tool_call.ts`, `cli/src/core/spine.ts`, `cli/src/tools.ts`), verification (`cli/src/core/verify*.ts`), operations (`cli/src/core/operation*.ts`).

Hard constraints every plan must respect:
- The approval gates, verification-path protection, managed policy and the VERIFIED outcome ladder are authorities no new surface may weaken (gate G-3: a client, hook, plugin, schedule or policy must not bypass a gate). PF-3 in particular adds a listener: the plan must say who can connect (same uid only, by socket permissions and directory permissions), what the token protects against, what a second client may and may not do (may it answer an approval the first client was asked? decide conservatively), and why DNS-rebinding/CSRF cannot reach a localhost HTTP/WebSocket listener if one exists at all (the conservative decision may be: unix socket only in v1.3.0, no TCP listener; say so if you take it and check it against the acceptance wording).
- A CI gate fails if `runTurnImpl`, `dispatchToolCallImpl`, `runSubagent`, `compactNowImpl` or `driveOperation` grow in cyclomatic complexity or nesting (`cli/critical-complexity-baseline.json`). MT-2 touches dispatch: plan it so those functions shrink or stay equal, and say how the baseline file is handled if a function is split (read `cli/scripts/check_critical_complexity.ts`: a renamed or missing function fails closed).
- Model-facing tool descriptions and the tool list have a size budget and exact-shape tests (`cli/test/context_convergence.test.ts`, `cli/test/lsp_shape.test.ts`, protocol parity tests): MT-2 must be behaviour-preserving for what the model sees; say which characterization tests pin that and which must be added first.
- Every new CLI command, setting, protocol message or file format needs docs (gate G-6 wants a runnable example per new surface, run in CI), a schema/version ledger entry where the repo keeps one, tests that fail when the guard is removed, and hostile cases.
- Tests run with a throwaway HOME, no network, no live inference (scripted gateway fixture `cli/test/helpers/fixtures.ts` `startGateway`); new test files register `cli/test/helpers/leak_guard.ts`; child processes are stopped by pid; sockets and listeners are closed.
- Linux x86_64 is the only release target. Node 22 and 24.
- PF-4: importing the library entry must have no side effects (no commander parse, no process.exit, no stdout writes, no reading of the real HOME at import time); the package must still build the same tarball layout (`scripts/package-linux.sh`, reproducibility check: the package is built twice and compared byte for byte in CI); D13 default = not published.

For EACH unit give: the acceptance verbatim; what exists that it builds on (file:line); the design (data model, commands/flags, protocol or file formats with exact shapes, state on disk and permissions, lifecycle, failure behaviour, limits); the security analysis; the exact list of files to add/change; the tests by name with what each proves (including hostile cases and, for refactors, the characterization tests that must be green before and after); docs and ledgers; and 2–4 mergeable slices in order, each independently green, with rough size (S/M/L) and the files touched, flagging hot files shared with other work (`cli/src/index.ts`, `cli/src/doctor.ts`, `cli/src/sidecar.ts`, `cli/src/core/dispatch_tool_call.ts`, `cli/src/core/run_turn.ts`, `cli/src/config.ts`, `cli/src/types.ts`). Keep each unit to what its acceptance needs and state what is out of scope for v1.3.0. Note dependencies between these units and on BG-1 (detached runs; planned separately: BG-1 may rely on PF-3's socket for live attach) and on GV-1/GV-5 (managed policy; being finished now).

Also record: a recommended build order across the five units with reasons (smallest and least entangled first; MT-2 is a wide refactor of hot files, so say when it is safest), reference-coding notes per `docs/XERJ_REFERENCE_CODING.md` (brief; "XERJ unavailable: <reason>" plus what you used is acceptable), risks, and open questions that could not be settled from the code.

Shell notes: zsh (use `bash -c` for loops); output is filtered by `rtk` (prefix `rtk proxy` when a grep/sed pipeline looks odd). Never read the real ~/.nexus, /etc/nexus or ~/.config/nexus.

Return (under 600 words): the file path; for each unit the slice list with sizes and hot files; the recommended build order; the decisions taken; the main risks; anything you could not determine. Be concrete enough that an implementer can start slice 1 of each unit from the plan alone.

## Workflow

### Plan
- Plan any non-trivial task (3+ steps or an architectural decision) before building: write the plan to `tasks/todo.md` as checkable items and check in before implementing. Plan the verification steps too.
- When something goes sideways, stop and re-plan at once.
- Tick items off as you go, give a high-level summary of each change, and end with a review section in `tasks/todo.md`.

### Subagents
- Keep the main context clean: offload research, exploration and parallel analysis to subagents, one tack per subagent. Throw more subagents at a complex problem.

### Lessons
- After any user correction, add the pattern to `tasks/lessons.md` as a rule that prevents the same mistake, and iterate until the mistake rate drops. Review the file at session start.

### Done means proven
- A task is complete when evidence shows it works: tests run, logs checked, behaviour diffed against main where relevant. Ask: would a staff engineer approve this?

### Elegance
- For a non-trivial change, pause and look for a more elegant way; when a fix feels hacky, implement the elegant solution with everything you now know. Keep simple, obvious fixes simple. Challenge your own work before presenting it.

### Bug reports
- Fix them from the evidence: logs, errors, failing tests, CI failures included. Resolve without being walked through it.

## Principles
- **Simplicity first**: the smallest change that works, touching only what is necessary.
- **Root cause**: no temporary fixes; senior-developer standard.

@RTK.md

# graphify
`/graphify` → invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` (`~/.claude/skills/graphify/SKILL.md`) before anything else.

# RTK (Rust Token Killer)

A hook rewrites shell commands through `rtk` (60-90% fewer tokens): write ordinary commands (`git status` runs as `rtk git status`).

- Raw output: `rtk proxy <cmd>`. Use it to debug, and whenever a rewritten `grep`, `awk` or `sed` pipeline returns filtered or odd output; rerun it raw before trusting it.
- Savings: `rtk gain`, `rtk gain --history`. Missed opportunities: `rtk discover`.
- If `rtk gain` fails, a different `rtk` is installed (reachingforthejack/rtk, Rust Type Kit); check `which rtk`.

## Principles

1. Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.
2. Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.
3. Touch only what you must. Clean up only your mess.
4. Define success criteria. Loop until verified.

## Agent workflow

Specialised agents live in `~/.claude/agents/` (their descriptions are in the agent list). Delegate any feature, bug fix or significant change to **`@orchestrator`**: it runs the pipeline and returns one structured summary (changes, test results, review findings, issues) while the verbose output stays in its context.

Pipeline: `@architect` plans and identifies affected files → `@coder` writes code (linter only, no tests) → `@tester` writes and runs tests, looping with coder on failures → `@reviewer` reviews the final diff (security, performance, readability, consistency) → `@design-qa` screenshots affected pages at mobile, tablet and desktop (UI changes only).

Call a single agent directly for one stage: architect, coder, tester, reviewer, design-qa, security-auditor, migration-planner (alembic, sqlite3), api-designer, ci-validator (GitLab CI).

Handle these yourself, without delegating: codebase questions, reading and explaining code, git operations, deployments, config changes.

Affected tests across all sub-projects (Go, Playwright, pytest): `./scripts/verify.sh` (the tester agent uses it).

## Browsing

Use the gstack `/browse` skill for all web browsing, and keep `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*` tools out of use.

## Sub-projects

| Project | Stack | Location |
|---------|-------|----------|
| SyndicateCode | Go 1.25, bubbletea TUI, gRPC, sqlite3 | `./SyndicateCode/` |
| aisyndicate | Next.js 16, React, TypeScript, Radix UI | `./aisyndicate/` |
| syndicateclaw | Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, alembic | `./syndicateclaw/` |
| controlplane-enterprise | Go, enterprise control plane | `./controlplane-enterprise/` |
| syndicategate | Go, backend service | `./syndicategate/` |

## graphify

`graphify-out/` holds a knowledge graph (god nodes, communities, cross-file relationships).

- For a codebase question, start with `graphify query "<question>"` when `graphify-out/graph.json` exists; use `graphify path "<A>" "<B>"` for relationships and `graphify explain "<concept>"` for one concept. Each returns a scoped subgraph, usually far smaller than `GRAPH_REPORT.md` or raw grep.
- Navigate broadly through `graphify-out/wiki/index.md` when it exists.
- Read `graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md` for broad architecture review, or when query, path and explain fall short.
- After modifying code, run `graphify update .` (AST-only, no API cost).

# nexus-code agent guide

TypeScript CLI (`cli/`), Rust core (`core/`), eval harness (`eval/`). Current plans: `docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`, then `docs/v1.3.0/PLAN.md`. Per-release records live in `docs/releases/` and `docs/evidence/`.

## Build and test
- Build: `make build` (core, then `tsc` in `cli/`). Everything: `make test`; the CI-equivalent run: `make test-ci`. Lint the core with `cargo clippy`; `cli/` has no lint script, `npm --prefix cli run build` type-checks it.
- One TypeScript test file: `cd cli && HOME=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx --test test/<name>.test.ts`. A throwaway `HOME` is mandatory: a test that touched the real `HOME` once overwrote `~/.config/nexus/config.env`.
- Done = the affected test files pass, plus `tsc` for TypeScript changes. CI is the arbiter; a failure that appears only locally comes from host state first (an unbuilt `cli/dist` or Rust core, a stray `/tmp/.git`), so rule that out before calling it a defect.
- Test-runner or process-handling changes run on Node 22 and 24: the two emit different `node:test` events.
- Rust builds use an isolated `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` per worktree.
- Preserve existing comments and unrelated changes.
- Entire CLI: export `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` before any `entire` command. The Entire gate no longer counts toward merging.

## Reference coding with XERJ (required)
- Before writing non-trivial code that has a peer-project analogue (feature, protocol, parser, worktree or provider handling, tool, test harness), read what mature projects do: query the local XERJ node, then record what you took, borrowed or rejected in the PR's "Reference coding" section. Exempt: trivial edits, doc-only changes, fixes fully specified by a failing test.
- Node, commands, corpora, licence and privacy rules, the field report, and the fallback when XERJ is unavailable ("XERJ unavailable: <reason>" plus `git grep`): `docs/XERJ_REFERENCE_CODING.md`. Read it when you start that first query.

## Concurrency, claims and release authority
- Several agents can work here: follow `docs/v1.0.0/CONCURRENCY.md`. Claim a slice or hot file under `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/nexus-claims/` before editing; one worktree and branch per slice (`~/nexus-wt/`), never `~/nexus-code` itself; isolate `HOME` for every test or probe; stop a process by its own pid, never `pkill -f`; check `git log` for foreign commits before each commit.
- Take the `GATEWAY` claim for any inference run; the key comes from the environment (`~/.config/nexus/config.env`) and is never printed. The gateway is the only live provider.
- Push, tag and publish only on an explicit owner instruction; release authority is the owner's.

## Merging and releasing
Bias to correct: a green PR is not a green `main`, and a pushed tag cannot be taken back.
- When merging: required checks are `test-matrix (22)`, `test-matrix (24)`, `linux-x86_64`; read each check's conclusion (empty or in-progress is not success). Merge with a merge commit, `gh pr merge <n> --merge --match-head-commit <full-sha>`. PRs that touch one subsystem merge one at a time, each followed by the CI run on `main`: two PRs green alone can break `main` together.
- When a PR's checks look wrong after `main` moved: PR checks run on GitHub's merge commit, so confirm the run checked out the current `merge_commit_sha` (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n> --jq .merge_commit_sha`); a stale one tests old content.
- When cutting a stable release: make a version-only commit directly on the accepted RC (`node scripts/check-version-only-diff.mjs <rc-ref> <stable-ref>`), land it on `main` through a merge-commit PR, and only then tag, because `release.yml` requires the tagged commit to be an ancestor of `main`. Version tags are immutable: re-run a failed run, or move to the next RC or patch. Then follow `docs/RELEASE_PROCESS.md`.
- When reporting a gate or a result: state it as measured ("ledger closed, qualification pending"), record failed runs unaltered, and make no frontier-grade claim without external qualification.
- Before tagging or merging, check: required checks green at the exact head? CI on `main` green after the previous merge? Tagged commit an ancestor of `main`? Claims match the evidence?

# nexus-code agent guide

TypeScript CLI (`cli/`), Rust core (`core/`), eval harness (`eval/`). Current plans: `docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`, then `docs/v1.3.0/PLAN.md`. Per-release records live in `docs/releases/` and `docs/evidence/`.

## Build and test
- Build: `make build` (core, then `tsc` in `cli/`). Everything: `make test`; the CI-equivalent run: `make test-ci`. Lint the core with `cargo clippy`; `cli/` has no lint script, `npm --prefix cli run build` type-checks it.
- One TypeScript test file: `cd cli && HOME=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx --test test/<name>.test.ts`. A throwaway `HOME` is mandatory: a test that touched the real `HOME` once overwrote `~/.config/nexus/config.env`.
- Done = the affected test files pass, plus `tsc` for TypeScript changes. CI is the arbiter; a failure that appears only locally comes from host state first (an unbuilt `cli/dist` or Rust core, a stray `/tmp/.git`), so rule that out before calling it a defect.
- Test-runner or process-handling changes run on Node 22 and 24: the two emit different `node:test` events.
- Rust builds use an isolated `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` per worktree.
- Preserve existing comments and unrelated changes.
- Entire CLI: export `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` before any `entire` command. The Entire gate no longer counts toward merging.

## Reference coding with XERJ (required)
- Before writing non-trivial code that has a peer-project analogue (feature, protocol, parser, worktree or provider handling, tool, test harness), read what mature projects do: query the local XERJ node, then record what you took, borrowed or rejected in the PR's "Reference coding" section. Exempt: trivial edits, doc-only changes, fixes fully specified by a failing test.
- Node, commands, corpora, licence and privacy rules, the field report, and the fallback when XERJ is unavailable ("XERJ unavailable: <reason>" plus `git grep`): `docs/XERJ_REFERENCE_CODING.md`. Read it when you start that first query.

## Concurrency, claims and release authority
- Several agents can work here: follow `docs/v1.0.0/CONCURRENCY.md`. Claim a slice or hot file under `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/nexus-claims/` before editing; one worktree and branch per slice (`~/nexus-wt/`), never `~/nexus-code` itself; isolate `HOME` for every test or probe; stop a process by its own pid, never `pkill -f`; check `git log` for foreign commits before each commit.
- Take the `GATEWAY` claim for any inference run; the key comes from the environment (`~/.config/nexus/config.env`) and is never printed. The gateway is the only live provider.
- Push, tag and publish only on an explicit owner instruction; release authority is the owner's.

## Merging and releasing
Bias to correct: a green PR is not a green `main`, and a pushed tag cannot be taken back.
- When merging: required checks are `test-matrix (22)`, `test-matrix (24)`, `linux-x86_64`; read each check's conclusion (empty or in-progress is not success). Merge with a merge commit, `gh pr merge <n> --merge --match-head-commit <full-sha>`. PRs that touch one subsystem merge one at a time, each followed by the CI run on `main`: two PRs green alone can break `main` together.
- When a PR's checks look wrong after `main` moved: PR checks run on GitHub's merge commit, so confirm the run checked out the current `merge_commit_sha` (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n> --jq .merge_commit_sha`); a stale one tests old content.
- When cutting a stable release: make a version-only commit directly on the accepted RC (`node scripts/check-version-only-diff.mjs <rc-ref> <stable-ref>`), land it on `main` through a merge-commit PR, and only then tag, because `release.yml` requires the tagged commit to be an ancestor of `main`. Version tags are immutable: re-run a failed run, or move to the next RC or patch. Then follow `docs/RELEASE_PROCESS.md`.
- When reporting a gate or a result: state it as measured ("ledger closed, qualification pending"), record failed runs unaltered, and make no frontier-grade claim without external qualification.
- Before tagging or merging, check: required checks green at the exact head? CI on `main` green after the previous merge? Tagged commit an ancestor of `main`? Claims match the evidence?

# nexus-code agent guide

TypeScript CLI (`cli/`), Rust core (`core/`), eval harness (`eval/`). Current plans: `docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`, then `docs/v1.3.0/PLAN.md`. Per-release records live in `docs/releases/` and `docs/evidence/`.

## Build and test
- Build: `make build` (core, then `tsc` in `cli/`). Everything: `make test`; the CI-equivalent run: `make test-ci`. Lint the core with `cargo clippy`; `cli/` has no lint script, `npm --prefix cli run build` type-checks it.
- One TypeScript test file: `cd cli && HOME=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx --test test/<name>.test.ts`. A throwaway `HOME` is mandatory: a test that touched the real `HOME` once overwrote `~/.config/nexus/config.env`.
- Done = the affected test files pass, plus `tsc` for TypeScript changes. CI is the arbiter; a failure that appears only locally comes from host state first (an unbuilt `cli/dist` or Rust core, a stray `/tmp/.git`), so rule that out before calling it a defect.
- Test-runner or process-handling changes run on Node 22 and 24: the two emit different `node:test` events.
- Rust builds use an isolated `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` per worktree.
- Preserve existing comments and unrelated changes.
- Entire CLI: export `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` before any `entire` command. The Entire gate no longer counts toward merging.

## Reference coding with XERJ (required)
- Before writing non-trivial code that has a peer-project analogue (feature, protocol, parser, worktree or provider handling, tool, test harness), read what mature projects do: query the local XERJ node, then record what you took, borrowed or rejected in the PR's "Reference coding" section. Exempt: trivial edits, doc-only changes, fixes fully specified by a failing test.
- Node, commands, corpora, licence and privacy rules, the field report, and the fallback when XERJ is unavailable ("XERJ unavailable: <reason>" plus `git grep`): `docs/XERJ_REFERENCE_CODING.md`. Read it when you start that first query.

## Concurrency, claims and release authority
- Several agents can work here: follow `docs/v1.0.0/CONCURRENCY.md`. Claim a slice or hot file under `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/nexus-claims/` before editing; one worktree and branch per slice (`~/nexus-wt/`), never `~/nexus-code` itself; isolate `HOME` for every test or probe; stop a process by its own pid, never `pkill -f`; check `git log` for foreign commits before each commit.
- Take the `GATEWAY` claim for any inference run; the key comes from the environment (`~/.config/nexus/config.env`) and is never printed. The gateway is the only live provider.
- Push, tag and publish only on an explicit owner instruction; release authority is the owner's.

## Merging and releasing
Bias to correct: a green PR is not a green `main`, and a pushed tag cannot be taken back.
- When merging: required checks are `test-matrix (22)`, `test-matrix (24)`, `linux-x86_64`; read each check's conclusion (empty or in-progress is not success). Merge with a merge commit, `gh pr merge <n> --merge --match-head-commit <full-sha>`. PRs that touch one subsystem merge one at a time, each followed by the CI run on `main`: two PRs green alone can break `main` together.
- When a PR's checks look wrong after `main` moved: PR checks run on GitHub's merge commit, so confirm the run checked out the current `merge_commit_sha` (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n> --jq .merge_commit_sha`); a stale one tests old content.
- When cutting a stable release: make a version-only commit directly on the accepted RC (`node scripts/check-version-only-diff.mjs <rc-ref> <stable-ref>`), land it on `main` through a merge-commit PR, and only then tag, because `release.yml` requires the tagged commit to be an ancestor of `main`. Version tags are immutable: re-run a failed run, or move to the next RC or patch. Then follow `docs/RELEASE_PROCESS.md`.
- When reporting a gate or a result: state it as measured ("ledger closed, qualification pending"), record failed runs unaltered, and make no frontier-grade claim without external qualification.
- Before tagging or merging, check: required checks green at the exact head? CI on `main` green after the previous merge? Tagged commit an ancestor of `main`? Claims match the evidence?

# Nexus Code v1.3 plan: the platform track

Status: PLAN, written 2026-11-15 against `main` plus the v1.2.0-rc.1 notes, at the owner's request ("draft the v1.3 platform track as recommended"). Amended 2026-11-23 with Codex-derived units SB-1, MT-2 and VR-3 (and an explicit MT-1 row). It follows v1.2.1 and v1.2.2 ([`docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`](../v1.2.1/PLAN.md), decision D12). Nothing here is a claim that Nexus Code is frontier-grade, and no unit starts without the decisions in section 7.

## 1. Purpose and theme

Frontier clients are platforms: a CLI plus a desktop app, IDE integration, background and scheduled agents, an SDK or managed API, installable plugin bundles, and enterprise policy (web sources of 2026-11-15, mostly third-party; see [`docs/v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md`](../v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md) §2). Nexus is a single-binary Linux CLI and TUI. It cannot match breadth or first-party model fit, and a worse copy of three funded platforms is not a goal.

The v1.3 theme: **let other programs drive Nexus and let teams govern it, without weakening the gate.** Every new surface (an IDE over ACP, a scheduler, a hook, a plugin, an SDK caller, a managed policy) goes through the same approval and verification gates as the terminal does. The differentiator to build on is the one nobody else ships by default: a completion you can audit (independent verification, receipts, evidence). Two consequences shape the plan:

1. **Nexus as the verification layer for other harnesses.** `nexus verify` and an MCP/ACP `verify` tool let a Codex, Claude Code or Aider session ask Nexus to independently check its work. This costs little (the machinery exists) and is positioned where the platforms are weakest.
2. **Governance as a product.** Managed policy with fixed precedence, a hash-chained and optionally signed audit export, and hooks that can only tighten.

Non-goals: a marketplace, a desktop or mobile app, a Nexus-specific VS Code extension (ACP clients already exist), hosted or multi-tenant operation (dropped 2026-11-15, decision D8), plugin auto-update, any new runtime dependency without a decision.

## 2. Evidence and its limits

- **Nexus today** (read-only inventory, 2026-11-15; "present" means present in source or docs, nothing was run): sidecar/TUI protocol is NDJSON over the sidecar's stdio with `PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1`, an event `v`, a one-way `hello`, typed unions in `cli/src/protocol.ts:53-204` hand-mirrored in `core/src/bin/nexus_tui/protocol.rs`, **no schema file, no socket**; `nexus run --json` returns `TaskExecutionResult` (`cli/src/core/app.ts:44`) with no schema or version, exit codes defined only in code (0 verified, 2 completed-unverified, 130 interrupted, 1 otherwise); `ApplicationCore` is an accidental re-export (`cli/src/index.ts:1240`) and `cli/package.json` has `main` and `bin` but no `exports` or `types`; operations are durable and resumable (per-operation lock, 12 h wait survives restart, `maxConcurrentUnits` capped at 64 and clamped to 1 without `git.isolate`) but **foreground-only**, with no scheduler, cron, trigger or daemon in the code; plugins are plain JS modules with no manifest, checksum or install command, workspace plugins load after `nexus trust` with full process authority, hooks cover pre/post tool only; policy is the workspace-local `.nexus-security.json`, **fails open to defaults on a parse error**, with no system or admin layer; session export is `nexus-session-export/2` reachable only through `/export`; the flight log is append-only by convention (no hash chain found) and the CERI evidence store hashes files but has no signature or verify command; local OTLP-style traces are written on every session with no opt-in gate and no network exporter found; a goal (objective ledger) persists across sessions via `--resume`, but nothing re-launches a task on its own.
- **Peers, read from source** (shallow clones of 2026-11-13/14; Codex at commit 336b19a; untrusted code, nothing run): ACP servers in goose (`crates/goose/src/acp`), Cline (`apps/cli/src/acp/acpAgent.ts`), Gemini CLI (`packages/cli/src/acp`) and opencode (`packages/cli/src/acp/agent.ts`), the Codex `app-server` (JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio, websocket or UDS; schema generated from Rust types and checked in); schedulers in goose (`scheduler/full.rs`), Cline (`*.cron.md` and event specs) and opencode (a `ScheduleTable` with `in`/`at`/`every`/`cron` and an optional deterministic wake `check`); hooks in Gemini CLI (`docs/hooks/reference.md`), goose (`hooks/mod.rs`), Cline and Codex; extension manifests in Gemini CLI (`gemini-extension.json`), goose (Open Plugins and Gemini formats) and opencode; policy tiers in Gemini CLI (`core/src/policy/config.ts:67-71`), opencode (`managed-policy.ts`) and Codex (`requirements.toml`); goal state in opencode (`schema/src/goal.ts`) and Codex (`thread/goal/*`).

- **Research notes** (2026-11-15): the Anthropic 2026 agentic coding trends report (read in full; a vendor document with no methodology, customer-reported figures) and OpenHands (documentation, not source) support three priorities here: VR-1 and VR-2 (the report's own evidence is that people delegate what is cheaply checkable, so verifiability is the delegation boundary), PA-1 (it names a view of concurrent agent sessions) and AC-1 (above). They are framing, not evidence about Nexus.
- **Not covered:** Claude Code and agy were not read (web sources only); parts of Cline's daemon, Codex's hook handler types and plugin manifest, and goose's managed policy were sampled, not read in full; peer behaviour under load was not measured.

## 3. Principles

1. **Protocol first.** Nothing else in this plan is safe to build until the client protocol is published, schema'd, versioned and conformance-tested.
2. **One gate.** A new surface can request an approval but can never answer one on behalf of Nexus's own gates (SI-2, CS-* rules, verification). A client that answers "allow" to a denied action must have no effect; this is tested.
3. **Tighten only.** Hooks and managed policy may deny, require a human, or rewrite arguments toward safer values. They never grant.
4. **Unattended means stricter.** Scheduled and detached runs never get allow-always, run in a fresh worktree, and record that they were unattended in every receipt.
5. **Explicit trust.** Project-defined hooks, plugins and policy run only after a trust decision keyed by a content hash; a changed file asks again.
6. **Schemas come from types.** Generate JSON Schema from the TypeScript types and check it in with a parity test, so the Rust mirror cannot drift (reference: Codex `app-server-protocol` schema export, goose `acp-schema.json`).
7. **No new runtime dependency** without a decision. ACP is plain JSON-RPC; hash chains and ed25519 signing use `node:crypto`.
8. **Experimental is a flag.** New methods sit behind `experimental` at `initialize` (reference: Codex `experimentalApi`) until a conformance suite has run against two real clients.

| D22 | Permission profile names and defaults (SB-1): which named profiles ship, whether `:workspace` is the interactive default, and whether managed policy may force a stricter profile | ship `:workspace`, `:read-only`, `:network`; interactive default stays today's engine defaults until an explicit profile is set; managed policy may force a stricter profile, never a looser one |

## 8. Risks

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| A new socket or listener widens the attack surface | unix socket mode 0600 by default; token and origin check for any HTTP listener; G-3 |
| A client answers approvals in a way that bypasses a gate | the gate decides first; the client only supplies a human's yes or no; G-3 tests it |
| Fail-closed policy locks an operator out | a clear message naming the file and tier, and a documented recovery path; tested |
| Unattended runs burn the shared gateway or contend with live measurements | schedules use the `GATEWAY` claim protocol; read-only default; run budget in every spec |
| Plugin supply chain | commit-pinned installs, capabilities shown, no auto-update, install receipt, `verify` |
| Protocol churn after publication | `experimental` flag, version range in `hello`, schema diff in CI |
| Scope: this track is as large as v1.2.0 plus v1.2.1 | the sequencing above; Phase D rolls without ceremony; a unit is never half-merged |
| An unreviewed peer assumption | sources and limits are listed in section 2; each unit's PR repeats the reference coding record (XERJ queries, what was taken or rejected) |
| Permission profiles look like a grant surface | profiles only rename and bundle existing confinement; they cannot weaken CS-9, verification-path protection, or managed policy; G-3 covers a hostile profile string |
| Tool-registry refactor regresses a gate | behaviour-preserving slices w

content.content:
1	# Nexus Code v1.3 plan: the platform track
2	
3	Status: PLAN, written 2026-11-15 against `main` plus the v1.2.0-rc.1 notes, at the owner's request ("draft the v1.3 platform track as recommended"). Amended 2026-11-23 with Codex-derived units SB-1, MT-2 and VR-3 (and an explicit MT-1 row). It follows v1.2.1 and v1.2.2 ([`docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`](../v1.2.1/PLAN.md), decision D12). Nothing here is a claim that Nexus Code is frontier-grade, and no unit starts without the decisions in section 7.
4	
5	## 1. Purpose and theme
6	
7	Frontier clients are platforms: a CLI plus a desktop app, IDE integration, background and scheduled agents, an SDK or managed API, installable plugin bundles, and enterprise policy (web sources of 2026-11-15, mostly third-party; see [`docs/v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md`](../v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md) §2). Nexus is a single-binary Linux CLI and TUI. It cannot match breadth or first-party model fit, and a worse copy of three funded platforms is not a goal.
8	
9	The v1.3 theme: **let other programs drive Nexus and let teams govern it, without weakening the gate.** Every new surface (an IDE over ACP, a scheduler, a hook, a plugin, an SDK caller, a managed policy) goes through the same approval and verification gates as the terminal does. The differentiator to build on is the one nobody else ships by default: a completion you can audit (independent verification, receipts, evidence). Two consequences shape the plan:
10	
11	1. **Nexus as the verification layer for other harnesses.** `nexus verify` and an MCP/ACP `verify` tool let a Codex, Claude Code or Aider session ask Nexus to independently check its work. This costs little (the machinery exists) and is positioned where the platforms are weakest.
12	2. **Governance as a product.** Managed policy with fixed precedence, a hash-chained and optionally signed audit export, and hooks that can only tighten.
13	
14	Non-goals: a marketplace, a desktop or mobile app, a Nexus-specific VS Code extension (ACP clients already exist), hosted or multi-tenant operation (dropped 2026-11-15, decision D8), plugin auto-update, any new runtime dependency without a decision.
15	
16	## 2. Evidence and its limits
17	
18	- **Nexus today** (read-only inventory, 2026-11-15; "present" means present in source or docs, nothing was run): sidecar/TUI protocol is NDJSON over the sidecar's stdio with `PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1`, an event `v`, a one-way `hello`, typed unions in `cli/src/protocol.ts:53-204` hand-mirrored in `core/src/bin/nexus_tui/protocol.rs`, **no schema file, no socket**; `nexus run --json` returns `TaskExecutionResult` (`cli/src/core/app.ts:44`) with no schema or version, exit codes defined only in code (0 verified, 2 completed-unverified, 130 interrupted, 1 otherwise); `ApplicationCore` is an accidental re-export (`cli/src/index.ts:1240`) and `cli/package.json` has `main` and `bin` but no `exports` or `types`; operations are durable and resumable (per-operation lock, 12 h wait survives restart, `maxConcurrentUnits` capped at 64 and clamped to 1 without `git.isolate`) but **foreground-only**, with no scheduler, cron, trigger or daemon in the code; plugins are plain JS modules with no manifest, checksum or install command, workspace plugins load after `nexus trust` with full process authority, hooks cover pre/post tool only; policy is the workspace-local `.nexus-security.json`, **fails open to defaults on a parse error**, with no system or admin layer; session export is `nexus-session-export/2` reachable only through `/export`; the flight log is append-only by convention (no hash chain found) and the CERI evidence store hashes files but has no signature or verify command; local OTLP-style traces are written on every session with no opt-in gate and no network exporter found; a goal (objective ledger) persists across sessions via `--resume`, but nothing re-launches a task on its own.
19	- **Peers, read from source** (shallow clones of 2026-11-13/14; Codex at commit 336b19a; untrusted code, nothing run): ACP servers in goose (`crates/goose/src/acp`), Cline (`apps/cli/src/acp/acpAgent.ts`), Gemini CLI (`packages/cli/src/acp`) and opencode (`packages/cli/src/acp/agent.ts`), the Codex `app-server` (JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio, websocket or UDS; schema generated from Rust types and checked in); schedulers in goose (`scheduler/full.rs`), Cline (`*.cron.md` and event specs) and opencode (a `ScheduleTable` with `in`/`at`/`every`/`cron` and an optional deterministic wake `check`); hooks in Gemini CLI (`docs/hooks/reference.md`), goose (`hooks/mod.rs`), Cline and Codex; extension manifests in Gemini CLI (`gemini-extension.json`), goose (Open Plugins and Gemini formats) and opencode; policy tiers in Gemini CLI (`core/src/policy/config.ts:67-71`), opencode (`managed-policy.ts`) and Codex (`requirements.toml`); goal state in opencode (`schema/src/goal.ts`) and Codex (`thread/goal/*`).
20	- **Codex re-read** (2026-11-23; sparse clone of [openai/codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) at `e0a6d05`, Apache-2.0; untrusted code, nothing run; XERJ hub had no `openai/codex` corpus): OS-native sandboxing behind named **permission profiles** (workspace-write roots, broad host reads, network off or managed/transparent TCP; Linux bwrap+seccomp, macOS Seatbelt, Windows restricted token) with explicit residual documentation (e.g. ignored `node_modules` injection); Starlark **execpolicy** `prefix_rule` with load-time `match`/`not_match` examples (already the model for CS-9 `command_rules.ts`); centralized **tool registry/router/orchestrator** (spec + handler bound together; approve → sandbox → run → hooks; parallel batch); app-server **schema-from-types** export to checked-in JSON Schema and TypeScript; sandbox **violation** recording as first-class events. **Took for v1.3 units SB-1, MT-2, VR-3** (below): profile productization without loosening gates; registry-shaped tool dispatch; denial/violation receipts. **Rejected:** ChatGPT/cloud auth and task crates; treating sandbox confinement alone as completion trust (Nexus’s differentiator remains the verification ladder); copying code verbatim.
21	- **XERJ reference queries** (2026-11-15, local node, read-only; the `opencode` index is flagged "not verified complete", so a miss there is not proof of absence): `xerj code opencode` for ACP, scheduling and plugin manifests; `xerj search --prefix goose` for ACP, scheduler and extension manifests; `xerj search --prefix xc-opencode` for managed policy. **Took:** opencode's wire-level ACP fixture pattern (`packages/cli/test/acp/wire-fixture.ts`) for protocol conformance tests; opencode's schedule model (`schema/src/schedule.ts`, `core/src/schedule/sql.ts`: `next_due_at`, `remaining_runs`, `last_outcome`, deterministic wake check with hard limits) and its documented GitHub scheduled-workflow example; goose's cron-on-a-recipe scheduler shape (`scheduler/full.rs`, `commands/schedule.rs`); goose's checked-in ACP schema and method metadata (`acp-meta.json`); goose's plugin formats (`plugins/formats/gemini.rs`, `open_plugins.rs`); opencode's managed policy as config statements with an action, a resource and an effect (`config/plugin/policy.ts`). **Rejected:** opencode's in-process Effect plugin hooks (a JS-in-process model is what Nexus is trying to move away from), goose's per-run `Auto` mode for scheduled runs (unattended runs must never get allow-always), and any code copied verbatim: reference code is read-only inspiration.
22	- **Research notes** (2026-11-15): the Anthropic 2026 agentic coding trends report (read in full; a vendor document with no methodology, customer-reported figures) and OpenHands (documentation, not source) support three priorities here: VR-1 and VR-2 (the report's own evidence is that people delegate what is cheaply checkable, so verifiability is the delegation boundary), PA-1 (it names a view of concurrent agent sessions) and AC-1 (above). They are framing, not evidence about Nexus.
23	- **Not covered:** Claude Code and agy were not read (web sources only); parts of Cline's daemon, Codex's hook handler types and plugin manifest, and goose's managed policy were sampled, not read in full; peer behaviour under load was not measured.
24	
25	## 3. Principles
26	
27	1. **Protocol first.** Nothing else in this plan is safe to build until the client protocol is published, schema'd, versioned and conformance-tested.
28	2. **One gate.** A new surface can request an approval but can never answer one on behalf of Nexus's own gates (SI-2, CS-* rules, verification). A client that answers "allow" to a denied action must have no effect; this is tested.
29	3. **Tighten only.** Hooks and managed policy may deny, require a human, or rewrite arguments toward safer values. They never grant.
30	4. **Unattended means stricter.** Scheduled and detached runs never get allow-always, run in a fresh worktree, and record that they were unattended in every receipt.
31	5. **Explicit trust.** Project-defined hooks, plugins and policy run only after a trust decision keyed by a content hash; a changed file asks again.
32	6. **Schemas come from types.** Generate JSON Schema from the TypeScript types and check it in with a parity test, so the Rust mirror cannot drift (reference: Codex `app-server-protocol` schema export, goose `acp-schema.json`).
33	7. **No new runtime dependency** without a decision. ACP is plain JSON-RPC; hash chains and ed25519 signing use `node:crypto`.
34	8. **Experimental is a flag.** New methods sit behind `experimental` at `initialize` (reference: Codex `experimentalApi`) until a conformance suite has run against two real clients.
35	
36	## 4. Workstreams and units
37	
38	Size: S = one PR; M = two to four PRs; L = a program. P0 = prerequisite, P1 = core, P2 = stretch.
39

140	|---|---|---|
141	| D13 | Publish an npm package or SDK (PF-4)? Package name and licence; external publishing is yours to authorise | no publish; the entry point is documented but not published |
142	| D14 | Which two ACP clients to test against (AC-2) | the two most widely used open-source ones that run on Linux without an account |
143	| D15 | Detached runner model: a documented `systemd --user` unit, or a self-daemonizing mode (BG-1) | the `systemd --user` unit only |
144	| D16 | System policy location and whether the system and user tiers fail closed on a parse error (GV-1) | `/etc/nexus/policy.toml`; fail closed |
145	| D17 | Audit signing: where the operator's ed25519 key lives and whether signing is required or optional (GV-2) | optional; key path supplied by the operator, never stored by Nexus |
146	| D18 | Whether in-process workspace JS plugins stay supported after HK-1/HK-2 (HK-3) | keep, but move to per-plugin trust with a deprecation note |
147	| D19 | Unattended-run defaults (BG-2): `read-only` only, or `worktree-write` allowed | `read-only` by default; `worktree-write` per schedule with an explicit flag |
148	| D20 | Position Nexus as a verifier for other harnesses (VR-2)? | yes |
149	| D21 | Event triggers and remote (SSH) execution: v1.4 or never | v1.4 candidate, no work in v1.3 |
150	| D22 | Permission profile names and defaults (SB-1): which named profiles ship, whether `:workspace` is the interactive default, and whether managed policy may force a stricter profile | ship `:workspace`, `:read-only`, `:network`; interactive default stays today's engine defaults until an explicit profile is set; managed policy may force a stricter profile, never a looser one |
151	
152	## 8. Risks
153	
154	| Risk | Mitigation |
155	|---|---|
156	| A new socket or listener widens the attack surface | unix socket mode 0600 by default; token and origin check for any HTTP listener; G-3 |
157	| A client answers approvals in a way that bypasses a gate | the gate decides first; the client only supplies a human's yes or no; G-3 tests it |
158	| Fail-closed policy locks an operator out | a clear message naming the file and tier, and a documented recovery path; tested |
159	| Unattended runs burn the shared gateway or contend with live measurements | schedules use the `GATEWAY` claim protocol; read-only default; run budget in every spec |
160	| Plugin supply chain | commit-pinned installs, capabilities shown, no auto-update, install receipt, `verify` |
161	| Protocol churn after publication | `experimental` flag, version range in `hello`, schema diff in CI |
162	| Scope: this track is as large as v1.2.0 plus v1.2.1 | the sequencing above; Phase D rolls without ceremony; a unit is never half-merged |
163	| An unreviewed peer assumption | sources and limits are listed in section 2; each unit's PR repeats the reference coding record (XERJ queries, what was taken or rejected) |
164	| Permission profiles look like a grant surface | profiles only rename and bundle existing confinement; they cannot weaken CS-9, verification-path protection, or managed policy; G-3 covers a hostile profile string |
165	| Tool-registry refactor regresses a gate | behaviour-preserving slices with focused dispatch + G-3 before merge; MT-2 never introduces allow-always or client-answered approvals |

# Nexus Code v1.3 plan: the platform track

Status: PLAN, written 2026-11-15 against `main` plus the v1.2.0-rc.1 notes, at the owner's request ("draft the v1.3 platform track as recommended"). Amended 2026-11-23 with Codex-derived units SB-1, MT-2 and VR-3 (and an explicit MT-1 row). It follows v1.2.1 and v1.2.2 ([`docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`](../v1.2.1/PLAN.md), decision D12). Nothing here is a claim that Nexus Code is frontier-grade, and no unit starts without the decisions in section 7.

## 1. Purpose and theme

Frontier clients are platforms: a CLI plus a desktop app, IDE integration, background and scheduled agents, an SDK or managed API, installable plugin bundles, and enterprise policy (web sources of 2026-11-15, mostly third-party; see [`docs/v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md`](../v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md) §2). Nexus is a single-binary Linux CLI and TUI. It cannot match breadth or first-party model fit, and a worse copy of three funded platforms is not a goal.

The v1.3 theme: **let other programs drive Nexus and let teams govern it, without weakening the gate.** Every new surface (an IDE over ACP, a scheduler, a hook, a plugin, an SDK caller, a managed policy) goes through the same approval and verification gates as the terminal does. The differentiator to build on is the one nobody else ships by default: a completion you can audit (independent verification, receipts, evidence). Two consequences shape the plan:

1. **Nexus as the verification layer for other harnesses.** `nexus verify` and an MCP/ACP `verify` tool let a Codex, Claude Code or Aider session ask Nexus to independently check its work. This costs little (the machinery exists) and is positioned where the platforms are weakest.
2. **Governance as a product.** Managed policy with fixed precedence, a hash-chained and optionally signed audit export, and hooks that can only tighten.

Non-goals: a marketplace, a desktop or mobile app, a Nexus-specific VS Code extension (ACP clients already exist), hosted or multi-tenant operation (dropped 2026-11-15, decision D8), plugin auto-update, any new runtime dependency without a decision.

## 2. Evidence and its limits

- **Nexus today** (read-only inventory, 2026-11-15; "present" means present in source or docs, nothing was run): sidecar/TUI protocol is NDJSON over the sidecar's stdio with `PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1`, an event `v`, a one-way `hello`, typed unions in `cli/src/protocol.ts:53-204` hand-mirrored in `core/src/bin/nexus_tui/protocol.rs`, **no schema file, no socket**; `nexus run --json` returns `TaskExecutionResult` (`cli/src/core/app.ts:44`) with no schema or version, exit codes defined only in code (0 verified, 2 completed-unverified, 130 interrupted, 1 otherwise); `ApplicationCore` is an accidental re-export (`cli/src/index.ts:1240`) and `cli/package.json` has `main` and `bin` but no `exports` or `types`; operations are durable and resumable (per-operation lock, 12 h wait survives restart, `maxConcurrentUnits` capped at 64 and clamped to 1 without `git.isolate`) but **foreground-only**, with no scheduler, cron, trigger or daemon in the code; plugins are plain JS modules with no manifest, checksum or install command, workspace plugins load after `nexus trust` with full process authority, hooks cover pre/post tool only; policy is the workspace-local `.nexus-security.json`, **fails open to defaults on a parse error**, with no system or admin layer; session export is `nexus-session-export/2` reachable only through `/export`; the flight log is append-only by convention (no hash chain found) and the CERI evidence store hashes files but has no signature or verify command; local OTLP-style traces are written on every session with no opt-in gate and no network exporter found; a goal (objective ledger) persists across sessions via `--resume`, but nothing re-launches a task on its own.
- **Peers, read from source** (shallow clones of 2026-11-13/14; Codex at commit 336b19a; untrusted code, nothing run): ACP servers in goose (`crates/goose/src/acp`), Cline (`apps/cli/src/acp/acpAgent.ts`), Gemini CLI (`packages/cli/src/acp`) and opencode (`packages/cli/src/acp/agent.ts`), the Codex `app-server` (JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio, websocket or UDS; schema generated from Rust types and checked in); schedulers in goose (`scheduler/full.rs`), Cline (`*.cron.md` and event specs) and opencode (a `ScheduleTable` with `in`/`at`/`every`/`cron` and an optional deterministic wake `check`); hooks in Gemini CLI (`docs/hooks/reference.md`), goose (`hooks/mod.rs`), Cline and Codex; extension manifests in Gemini CLI (`gemini-extension.json`), goose (Open Plugins and Gemini formats) and opencode; policy tiers in Gemini CLI (`core/src/policy/config.ts:67-71`), opencode (`managed-policy.ts`) and Codex (`requirements.toml`); goal state in opencode (`schema/src/goal.ts`) and Codex (`thread/goal/*`).
- **Codex re-read** (2026-11-23; sparse clone of [openai/codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) at `e0a6d05`, Apache-2.0; untrusted code, nothing run; XERJ hub had no `openai/codex` corpus): OS-native sandboxing behind named **permission profiles** (workspace-write roots, broad host reads, network off or managed/transparent TCP; Linux bwrap+seccomp, macOS Seatbelt, Windows restricted token) with explicit residual documentation (e.g. ignored `node_modules` injection); Starlark **execpolicy** `prefix_rule` with load-time `match`/`not_match` examples (already the model for CS-9 `command_rules.ts`); centralized **tool registry/router/orchestrator** (spec + handler bound together; approve → sandbox → run → hooks; parallel batch); app-server **schema-from-types** export to checked-in JSON Schema and TypeScript; sandbox **violation** recording as first-class events. **Took for v1.3 units SB-1, MT-2, VR-3** (below): profile productization without loosening gates; registry-shaped tool dispatch; denial/violation receipts. **Rejected:** ChatGPT/cloud auth and task crates; treating sandbox confinement alone as completion trust (Nexus’s differentiator remains the verification ladder); copying code verbatim.
- **XERJ reference queries** (2026-11-15, local node, read-only; the `opencode` index is flagged "not verified complete", so a miss there is not proof of absence): `xerj code opencode` for ACP, scheduling and plugin manifests; `xerj search --prefix goose` for ACP, scheduler and extension manifests; `xerj search --prefix xc-opencode` for managed policy. **Took:** opencode's wire-level ACP fixture pattern (`packages/cli/test/acp/wire-fixture.ts`) for protocol conformance tests; opencode's schedule model (`schema/src/schedule.ts`, `core/src/schedule/sql.ts`: `next_due_at`, `remaining_runs`, `last_outcome`, deterministic wake check with hard limits) and its documented GitHub scheduled-workflow example; goose's cron-on-a-recipe scheduler shape (`scheduler/full.rs`, `commands/schedule.rs`); goose's checked-in ACP schema and method metadata (`acp-meta.json`); goose's plugin formats (`plugins/formats/gemini.rs`, `open_plugins.rs`); opencode's managed policy as config statements with an action, a resource and an effect (`config/plugin/policy.ts`). **Rejected:** opencode's in-process Effect plugin hooks (a JS-in-process model is what Nexus is trying to move away from), goose's per-run `Auto` mode for scheduled runs (unattended runs must never get allow-always), and any code copied verbatim: reference code is read-only inspiration.
- **Research notes** (2026-11-15): the Anthropic 2026 agentic coding trends report (read in full; a vendor document with no methodology, customer-reported figures) and OpenHands (documentation, not source) support three priorities here: VR-1 and VR-2 (the report's own evidence is that people delegate what is cheaply checkable, so verifiability is the delegation boundary), PA-1 (it names a view of concurrent agent sessions) and AC-1 (above). They are framing, not evidence about Nexus.
- **Not covered:** Claude Code and agy were not read (web sources only); parts of Cline's daemon, Codex's hook handler types and plugin manifest, and goose's managed policy were sampled, not read in full; peer behaviour under load was not measured.

## 3. Principles

1. **Protocol first.** Nothing else in this plan is safe to build until the client protocol is published, schema'd, versioned and conformance-tested.
2. **One gate.** A new surface can request an approval but can never answer one on behalf of Nexus's own gates (SI-2, CS-* rules, verification). A client that answers "allow" to a denied action must have no effect; this is tested.
3. **Tighten only.** Hooks and managed policy may deny, require a human, or rewrite arguments toward safer values. They never grant.
4. **Unattended means stricter.** Scheduled and detached runs never get allow-always, run in a fresh worktree, and record that they were unattended in every receipt.
5. **Explicit trust.** Project-defined hooks, plugins and policy run only after a trust decision keyed by a content hash; a changed file asks again.
6. **Schemas come from types.** Generate JSON Schema from the TypeScript types and check it in with a parity test, so the Rust mirror cannot drift (reference: Codex `app-server-protocol` schema export, goose `acp-schema.json`).
7. **No new runtime dependency** without a decision. ACP is plain JSON-RPC; hash chains and ed25519 signing use `node:crypto`.
8. **Experimental is a flag.** New methods sit behind `experimental` at `initialize` (reference: Codex `experimentalApi`) until a conformance suite has run against two real clients.

## 4. Workstreams and units

Size: S = one PR; M = two to four PRs; L = a program. P0 = prerequisite, P1 = core, P2 = stretch.

### PF: protocol and embedding foundation

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PF-1 | Publish the client protocol: JSON Schema generated from `cli/src/protocol.ts`, a checked-in copy, a TS/Rust parity test replacing hand-sync, capability negotiation in `hello` / `initialize` (version range, `experimental` flag), `docs/PROTOCOL.md`; wire-level conformance fixtures (reference: opencode `packages/cli/test/acp/wire-fixture.ts`) | schema diff fails CI when a type changes without a version decision; a recorded session replays through the fixture harness | M | P0 |
| PF-2 | `nexus run --json` result schema with a `schema_version`, documented exit codes in the manual, `--input-json` or stdin for the task | schema validated in tests; a consumer test parses the output | S | P0 |
| PF-3 | Transport beyond a parent's stdio: a unix domain socket (default) with a token and origin check for any localhost HTTP/WebSocket listener (reference: goose `acp/transport/auth.rs`, constant-time compare); several clients may attach and reattach | a second client attaches to a running session; a wrong token is refused; the socket is mode 0600 | M | P1 |
| PF-4 | Library entry point: a `lib` entry that does not run commander on import, `exports` and `types` in `cli/package.json`, a package name decision, a documented minimal embedding example that spawns the sidecar | an example script runs a verified task through the entry point in CI | M | P1 |

### AC: ACP and IDE access

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AC-1 | ACP adapter over the sidecar protocol (stdio), hand-rolled JSON-RPC with no dependency: `initialize` with a capability list, `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/prompt`, `session/cancel`; streaming `tool_call` and `tool_call_update` with diff content; a `verification` update carrying receipt ids and verifier results; client-bound `session/request_permission` with allow-once and reject only (no "allow always" at first); one extension, `_nexus/receipt/get`. Reference: goose, Cline, opencode, Gemini CLI ACP servers and the Codex app-server (all four ACP servers use the same three-option permission request; opencode attaches the diff to the request so the user decides with the change in view). The host side exists too: OpenHands' Agent Canvas drives Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and OpenCode over ACP (docs, 2026-11-15), so an ACP server is what makes Nexus drivable by such hosts | a scripted ACP client completes a task; an `allow` reply to an action the gates deny has no effect (gate test G-3); the receipt is retrievable | L | P1 |
| AC-2 | ACP conformance: fixture suite plus runs against two real ACP clients (decision D14), recorded as fixtures; no live model | both clients complete the basic flow; fixtures committed | M | P1 |

This supersedes v1.2.1 unit RD-5 (ACP server mode), which moves here.

### VR: Nexus as the verification layer

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| VR-1 | `nexus verify` (no agent run): given a worktree or a base and head, run the discovered or configured verifier, the type-check evidence (CG-4), the verification-file guard and the independent reviewer, and print a verdict VERIFIED / REGRESSION_FREE / UNVERIFIED / BLOCKED with the receipt; exit code per the documented contract; usable as a CI gate (pairs with the v1.2.1 GitHub Action, RD-4) | a known-bad diff (weakened test) is not VERIFIED; the same diff produced by another harness gives the same verdict | M | P1 |
| VR-2 | Expose verification as an MCP tool and an ACP extension so another harness can call Nexus to check its own work (`serve-mcp` today exposes workspace tools, not verification); the caller can read the verdict but cannot change it | an external client's session gets a verdict and a receipt id; tampering with the request cannot raise the verdict | M | P1 (decision D20) |
| VR-3 | Sandbox denial and violation events as first-class receipt and flight records (engine, profile, FS/network reason when known); appear in GV-2 audit export and in hostile suites. Reference: Codex `sandboxing` violation backends. Never raises a verdict | a denied sandboxed command is named in the receipt with engine and reason; audit export includes it; no path turns a sandbox denial into VERIFIED | S | P1 |

### SB: sandbox profiles

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SB-1 | Named permission profiles (`:workspace`, `:read-only`, `:network` — exact names per decision D22) that map today's bwrap/docker flags, HOME mounts and network settings without loosening gates; profiles compose with approval mode and managed policy (GV-1); `nexus doctor` and session posture print the effective profile; document residual holes (broad host reads, ignored trees) honestly. Reference: Codex permission profiles and sandbox defaults write-up. Does not replace verification-path protection, CS-9 or the VERIFIED ladder | CLI and doctor show the effective profile; a profile cannot disable verification-path protection, grant allow-always, or bypass G-3; existing sandbox tests pass under profile aliases; residual holes are documented beside the profile | M | P1 |

### MT: maintainability and tool dispatch

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MT-1 | Split `agent.ts` so ACP, background runners and hooks can share the turn spine without importing the CLI entry (referenced from sequencing; land before or with AC-1 / BG-1) | AC-1 and BG-1 can drive a turn without `commander` side effects; existing turn suites green | M | P1 |
| MT-2 | Tool registry/router: one module builds the model-visible tool list and binds handlers; approve → sandbox → run → hooks on a single path (Codex `core/src/tools` registry/router/orchestrator shape, PR #4510). Behaviour-preserving refactor of `dispatch_tool_call.ts` and related wiring; enables GV-1, HK-1 and ACP projections without growing the dispatch file further | focused dispatch and G-3 suites green; adding a tool is a registered spec+handler pair; no new grant path | L | P1 |

### BG: background and scheduled runs

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BG-1 | Detached runner: a user-level job runner that owns durable operations so a run survives its CLI process (decision D15: a documented `systemd --user` unit versus a self-daemonizing mode); foreground mode unchanged | kill the CLI, the run continues and resumes cleanly; the SI-7 kill test passes against the runner | L | P1 |
| BG-2 | Schedules: a spec (trigger `cron`, `every` or `once`; objective ledger id; `max_rounds`; timeout; policy `read-only` or `worktree-write`; optional deterministic wake `check` command with hard limits, reference opencode `schedule/check.ts:23-39`: 30 s, 20 tool calls, 32 KB, cannot create schedules or worktrees) stored beside operations (`next_due_at`, `remaining_runs`, `last_outcome` as in opencode `core/src/schedule/sql.ts`); `nexus schedule add\|list\|rm\|run-now`; each run in a fresh worktree; unattended flag in every receipt; no allow-always; delivery is a receipt plus a pointer file | a scheduled run on a seeded failing verifier ends BLOCKED and says so; an unattended run asking for approval is denied, not blocked forever; missed runs are reported, not silently skipped | L | P1 |
| BG-3 | Event triggers (file change, webhook) | deferred: needs a trust and abuse model first | M | P2 (v1.4) |

### GV: governance

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GV-1 | Managed policy with fixed precedence **system > user > project**: `/etc/nexus/policy.toml` (path per decision D16), `~/.config/nexus/policy.toml`, then the existing `.nexus-security.json`; restrict-only semantics (deny, require a human, disable auto/yolo, allowlist MCP servers and plugins, set verification-path modes); the effective tier is printed beside every decision; a parse error in the system or user tier **fails closed**; a project policy file is hashed and a changed one asks again (reference: Gemini CLI tiers, MATCH/MISMATCH/NEW integrity check and system settings paths; opencode managed policy; Codex `requirements.toml`) | a project policy cannot loosen a system policy; a corrupted system policy refuses to start with a clear message instead of failing open; precedence table covered by tests | M | P1 |
| GV-2 | Audit export: `nexus audit export <task\|session>` writes a bundle (session export, receipts, evidence, verification attempts, flight log excerpt) with a manifest of SHA-256 hashes and a hash chain, optionally signed with an operator-provided ed25519 key (`node:crypto`, decision D17); `nexus audit verify` | a bundle with one altered byte fails verification and names the file; an unsigned bundle verifies by hash only and says so | M | P1 |
| GV-3 | Hash-chain the flight recorder and the verification-attempt log (today append-only by convention only) and verify the chain on `nexus flights replay` | truncating or editing a record is detected | S | P1 |
| GV-4 | Telemetry transparency (this also settles v1.2.1 unit PC-5): document what the local traces contain, add a setting to disable them and a retention limit, state plainly that nothing leaves the host (no network exporter found) | doc plus a test that no network call is made | S | P1 |
| GV-5 | Admin controls from the system policy: a strict mode that disables auto and full-access, an MCP and plugin allowlist | strict mode refuses `--yes` and `--mode auto` with the policy source named | S | P1 |

### HK: hooks and plugins

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HK-1 | Declarative command hooks: events `pre-tool`, `post-tool`, `pre-verify`, `post-verify`, `permission-request`, `session-start`, `session-end`, `stop`, `pre-compact`; JSON on stdin (`session_id`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`) and on stdout (`decision`, `reason`, `hookSpecificOutput`), exit 2 blocks with stderr as the reason, a timeout, a scrubbed environment (reuse `buildMcpEnvironment`), results written to the receipt. A hook may only deny or tighten arguments, never grant (Gemini CLI also ignores `allow` from lower tiers). Project-defined hooks need a trust decision keyed by a hash of the command (reference: Gemini CLI `trusted_hooks.json`, goose `hooks/mod.rs`, Codex hook trust). Handler types: command only (no peer shipped http, prompt or subagent handlers in what was read) | a hook that returns `allow` for a denied action has no effect; a changed project hook asks again; the contract is documented so existing hook scripts of that shape transfer | M | P1 |
| HK-2 | Plugin manifest `nexus-plugin.json` (name, version, declared contributions: hooks, skills, verifiers, MCP servers; required permissions); install from a local path or a git URL **pinned to a commit hash**; capabilities shown at install, resolved commit recorded in an install receipt; `nexus plugins install\|list\|remove\|verify`; no marketplace and no auto-update (reference: Gemini CLI `gemini-extension.json`, goose `.goose-plugin-install.json`). Skills load on a declared trigger and are not always-on (references: OpenHands trigger-based skills, the on-demand-loading guidance of `agent-rules-books`). Also fix the documented example in `docs/SKILLS_AND_PLUGINS.md` that does not match the code (`onTurnStart` positional arguments versus a context object) and stop swallowing plugin load errors silently | installing a plugin whose declared permissions exceed the system policy is refused; `verify` detects a modified install; a skill whose trigger did not fire adds nothing to the request (request-shape snapshot) | M | P1 |
| HK-3 | Per-plugin trust instead of per-directory, and run workspace-defined plugin hooks as subprocesses rather than in-process (a trusted workspace today runs every `.js` file in it with full process authority) | decision D18; migration note for existing plugins | M | P2 |

### PA: parallel agents and goals

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PA-1 | Parallel run visibility: `nexus operation watch` (CLI view first) showing units, worktrees and owners; a worktree owner id recorded in the receipt (reference: Codex `worktree` crate `owner` and `bind_thread`); a concurrency cap tied to a CPU and memory budget instead of a count only | two parallel units show their owners and states; the cap refuses a third when the budget is exhausted | M | P1 |
| PA-2 | Verified merge arbitration: when parallel units integrate, apply each diff, run verification on the merged tree, reject on failure. No peer read does more than isolate; this is where Nexus can differ | two units whose changes conflict semantically (each passes alone) fail verification on the merged tree and neither is integrated silently | M | P1 |
| PA-3 | Goal semantics: a ledger entry active from an earlier process resumes **paused** (opencode `goal.ts` boot id), stall counting by failure fingerprint and not turn count, completion decided only by a verifier receipt, an optional token budget rolling up from sub-operations (reference: Codex goal budget); `/team` leaves experimental only after PA-1 and PA-2 | stale goal resumes paused with a visible reason; a model "I am done" does not complete a goal | M | P2 |
| PA-4 | **Bounded delegation and workflow commands** (trail 428; [baseline](PA4_BASELINE.md)): extend transient `spawn_subagent` and durable operations with a shared validated delegation contract/outcome, enforce authority intersection and recursive/resource limits, then expose real `/goal`, `/loop`, and `/batch` lifecycles through REPL and TUI/sidecar. Reuse `TeamOrchestrator`, `ConvergenceScheduler`, `OperationStore`, `ResourceRegistry`, specialist profiles, provider recovery, completion evidence, and existing stagnation detectors; do not add a second scheduler or workflow store. `/goal` owns an immutable objective and requirement/evidence ledger; `/loop` is bounded and verifier-driven; `/batch` validates a task graph and maps it into existing work units. Parsing, cancellation, pause/resume, status, recovery, and provider-neutral fixtures are part of each command contract. Spec-format validation may proceed independently; lifecycle and shared-contract work depends on PA-1/PA-2 evidence and WP-P10-02, with `/goal` semantics aligned to PA-3. | prompt-only subagent compatibility; parent/profile/session authority intersection and enforced recursive limits; typed non-success and unknown-effect outcomes; each command has durable state, lifecycle controls, recovery and status through supported interfaces; dependency and workspace conflicts cannot silently complete or overwrite; deterministic verifiers and independent review gate acceptance; standard-contract mock plus existing local/cloud fixtures pass without provider changes | L (staged packages) | P1 |

## 5. Sequencing

Phase A (foundation, parallelisable): PF-1, PF-2, GV-4, VR-1, GV-3. These unblock the rest and cost little.
Phase B: AC-1, HK-1, GV-1, GV-2, PF-4, PA-2, VR-2, MT-1, VR-3, SB-1.
Phase C: BG-1, BG-2, HK-2, PF-3, AC-2, PA-1, GV-5, MT-2.
Phase D (stretch, may roll to v1.4): PA-3, HK-3, BG-3.
PA-4 is staged: the existing operation-spec validator can be reused independently; command lifecycles and shared delegation changes follow WP-P10-02 and verified PA-1/PA-2 gates. `/goal` must also satisfy PA-3 before promotion.
MT-2 follows MT-1 so the registry refactor targets the split spine; SB-1 may land beside GV-1 (profiles must not outrank managed policy). VR-3 can ship as soon as sandbox denials are stable under SB-1 aliases, or earlier against today's engines if the receipt shape is profile-agnostic.

Dependencies on earlier plans: v1.2.1 RD-3 (`stream-json` output) feeds PF-2; RD-4 (GitHub Action) pairs with VR-1; CS-9 (per-command approval rules, v1.2.2) and GV-1 must agree on rule semantics (allow < prompt < forbidden, deciding rule recorded); MT-1 (the `agent.ts` split) makes AC-1 and BG-1 much easier and should land first if possible; PR-* (provider registry) is independent; MQ-* (measurement) should publish at least one result before this release claims anything.

## 6. Release gates

| Gate | Condition |
|---|---|
| G-1 | `make test` green at the exact head; required CI green; main CI green on the merge commit |
| G-2 | Protocol conformance: schema parity test and the wire-fixture suite green; AC-1 passes against two real clients or the release says "experimental" |
| G-3 | **Gate-bypass suite:** a hostile client, hook, plugin, schedule or policy file cannot approve a denied action, raise a verdict, widen a policy tier, or remove a verification-file protection |
| G-4 | Unattended runs: tests show no allow-always, a fresh worktree, the unattended flag in receipts, and a kill-and-resume pass |
| G-5 | Audit round trip: export, verify, tamper one byte, verify fails and names the file |
| G-6 | Docs and examples for every new surface (`docs/PROTOCOL.md`, hooks, plugins, policy, schedules, audit) with runnable examples in CI |
| G-7 | Notes keep the framing: "ledger closed, qualification pending" unless an external result (E2 per the v1.2.1 plan §7) exists |

## 7. Decisions needed

| Id | Decision | Default if unanswered |
|---|---|---|
| D13 | Publish an npm package or SDK (PF-4)? Package name and licence; external publishing is yours to authorise | no publish; the entry point is documented but not published |
